questions.question_text: Shays' Rebellion exposed which weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
questions.option_b: the national government's inability to raise an army or enforce laws
questions.explanation: Under the Articles, Congress couldn't tax directly or fund a response to the uprising — the impotence that pushed elites toward the Constitutional Convention. There was no executive at all.

questions.question_text: Federalist No. 10 argues a large republic best controls faction because:
questions.option_b: a multiplicity of interests prevents any single faction from forming a tyrannical majority
questions.option_c: it eliminates the causes of faction
questions.explanation: Madison says the CAUSES of faction can't be removed without destroying liberty — you can only control EFFECTS by extending the sphere so no single interest dominates. A required-document staple.

questions.question_text: Brutus No. 1 would most likely object to:
questions.option_b: expansive use of the Necessary and Proper Clause for broad federal programs
questions.explanation: Brutus warned the Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses would let the national government swallow the states — the anti-federalist fear of consolidated power. Pair it against Federalist 10.

questions.question_text: Categorical grants differ from block grants in that categorical grants:
questions.option_b: come with specific conditions and federal strings
questions.explanation: Categorical = narrow purpose + conditions (federal steering); block = broad purpose + state discretion. Which grant type expands FEDERAL influence is the point being tested.

questions.question_text: Which power belongs exclusively to the Senate?
questions.option_d: choosing the president in an Electoral College deadlock
questions.explanation: Advice and consent — confirmations and treaties — is the Senate's alone. Revenue bills start in the House; the House impeaches while the Senate tries; the House picks the president in a deadlock.

questions.option_d: a ruling by the Chief Justice
questions.explanation: The filibuster exploits unlimited Senate debate; cloture (Rule XXII) needs 60 votes. The effect: most major legislation needs a 60-vote supermajority — a structural reason for gridlock.

questions.question_text: Congress can override a presidential veto with:
questions.option_a: a simple majority in both chambers
questions.option_b: a two-thirds vote in both chambers
questions.explanation: 2/3 of BOTH chambers — deliberately hard (overrides succeed under 5% of the time), making the veto threat a bargaining chip. Three-fourths belongs to constitutional amendment ratification.

questions.option_b: judicial review — courts may strike down laws conflicting with the Constitution
questions.explanation: Marshall declared it the judiciary's province 'to say what the law is' — a power not explicit in Article III. The irony: the Court built its strongest weapon while declining to act in the case at hand.

questions.question_text: Most Bill of Rights protections apply to the states through:
questions.option_b: selective incorporation via the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause
questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights originally bound only the federal government; the Court incorporates rights against states case by case through 14th Amendment due process (e.g., McDonald v. Chicago). 'Selective' = one right at a time.

questions.question_text: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected students' armbands because:
questions.option_a: schools aren't bound by the First Amendment
questions.option_b: symbolic speech is protected unless it substantially disrupts school
questions.explanation: 'Students don't shed their rights at the schoolhouse gate' — silent, passive symbolic speech is protected under the substantial-disruption test. Later cases (Hazelwood, Morse) carve exceptions.

questions.question_text: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned which precedent?
questions.explanation: Brown held separate facilities 'inherently unequal,' demolishing Plessy's 1896 doctrine under Equal Protection. Plessy builds the wall, Brown tears it down — and enforcement required executive action (Little Rock).

questions.question_text: Voters in primary elections, compared with general elections, tend to be:
questions.option_b: more ideologically extreme and more engaged
questions.explanation: Low-turnout primaries attract the most committed partisans, pushing candidates to the wings before the general-election pivot to the center. A stock explanation for polarization.

questions.question_text: Mandatory spending (Social Security, Medicare) constrains fiscal policymaking because it:
questions.option_b: grows automatically by formula, shrinking the discretionary share
questions.option_c: is set by the Federal Reserve
questions.explanation: Entitlements pay out by eligibility formula without yearly votes — now ~two-thirds of spending — so Congress fights over a thinner discretionary slice. 'Reauthorized annually' describes discretionary appropriations.

questions.question_text: Keynesian and supply-side economics differ chiefly in that Keynesians emphasize:
questions.option_a: tax cuts on producers to spur output
questions.option_b: managing aggregate demand through government spending
questions.option_d: a balanced budget at all times
questions.explanation: Keynesians use government spending to manage demand, especially in downturns; supply-siders favor tax/regulatory cuts to boost production. These map onto liberal and conservative fiscal ideologies.

questions.question_text: Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held that:
questions.option_a: corporations may donate unlimited sums directly to candidates
questions.option_b: independent expenditures by corporations and unions are protected speech that can't be capped
questions.explanation: The ruling protects INDEPENDENT expenditures (not coordinated with campaigns) as speech, enabling super PACs. Direct corporate contributions to candidates remain banned. The independent/direct distinction is key.

questions.question_text: Drawing district lines to dilute the opposing party's votes is called:
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering is the MANIPULATION; redistricting is the neutral process; reapportionment reallocates seats after the census. Baker v. Carr made districting justiciable ('one person, one vote').

questions.question_text: The strongest predictor of whether an individual votes is:
questions.explanation: Education tops every participation model — it builds civic skills, efficacy, and registration know-how, and correlates with age and income. Demographics explain turnout far better than geography.
